result.summary: Pausanias describes the sanctuaries near Mount Cronos at Olympia, including the temple of Ilithyia and Sosipolis, whose origin story involves a baby turned dragon. He then describes the Hippodamium, the stadium entrance, and the hippodrome with its starting mechanism and the horse-frightening Taraxippus, with its many explanations.

scenes.title: Mount Cronos and Sosipolis' temple
scenes.summary: Rites to Cronos on his mountain, and the temple of Ilithyia where Sosipolis is worshipped with strict rules for his priestess.

scenes.title: The child who became a dragon
scenes.summary: A woman offers her baby to Elis's army against the Arcadians; he turns into a dragon and the Arcadians flee.
scenes.stakes: Elis risks defeat by the invading Arcadian army.

scenes.title: Aphrodite, Hippodamium, and stadium entrance
scenes.summary: Pausanias lists the ruined Aphrodite temple, the Hippodamium, the Private entrance, seats of the Umpires and Endymion's tomb.

scenes.title: The hippodrome starting mechanism
scenes.summary: The ship-prow starting place with its bronze eagle and dolphin, and the staggered release of the horses, invented by Cleœtas.

scenes.title: Taraxippus, terror of horses
scenes.summary: Pausanias reports many explanations of the horse-frightening Taraxippus, compares others at the Isthmus and Nemea, and notes Hippodamia's statue.
scenes.stakes: Charioteers risk crashes and injury from the unexplained terror.

alias_notes.explanation: One view takes Taraxippus as a surname of Poseidon, god of horses.

notable_quotes.reason: Cleœtas's own inscription proudly claiming invention of the Olympic horse start.

analysis.text: Local cult and legend explain the sacred landscape; Pausanias weighs rival explanations of Taraxippus without settling them.
The passage preserves details of Olympia's hippodrome and its starting machinery, plus women's limited roles in the festival.

fun_facts.text: The hippodrome Pausanias describes has not survived; its site is thought to lie largely eroded by the Alpheios river.

language_notes.text: Basilæ means 'queens' in Greek; the term refers to a group of women (or officials) in Elis who performed this sacrifice.
Tutelary means guardian or protecting; Sosipolis is the protector of the city and people of Elis.
Lustral water is water used for ritual purification before sacred rites.
Libations are offerings of poured liquid; here wine is excluded from his cult, unlike most Greek worship.
The name Sosipolis means 'saviour of the city' in Greek, explaining why the Eleans gave the god this title after the victory.
The Altis was the sacred grove and precinct of Zeus at Olympia; here a walled enclosure is called the Hippodamium after Hippodamia.
Pelops, Hippodamia's husband, was angry because her sons killed his son Chrysippus, his illegitimate child; she then fled to Midea in Argolis.
"Umpires" translates the Hellanodicae, the Elean judges who presided over the games.
Demeter Chamyne's priestess is the one woman privileged to watch; the text notes that unmarried girls were allowed, unlike married women, who were barred.
Endymion, in Elean tradition, was an early king of Elis, said to have set his sons a race at Olympia for the kingdom.
Agnaptus means "unbent" or "unbroken"; it names the portico beside the starting-place.
The rope served as a barrier, held across the front of the teams until released.
"Clerk of the course" is the official who operated the starting device, which raised the eagle and dropped the dolphin as the signal.
Hippodrome is the horse-racing course at Olympia; its 'outlet' is where the chariots exit the course's side embankment.
Autochthon means a native 'sprung from the soil', a person said to be original to the land.
A cenotaph is an empty tomb, a monument to someone buried elsewhere.
Myrtilus was Œnomaus' charioteer; bribed by Pelops, he sabotaged the chariot, then Pelops killed him, so Pelops sought to appease his ghost.
'Evil eye' here means a harmful, malicious influence; a 'demon' is a spirit, not necessarily a devil.
Poseidon Hippius is Poseidon as 'horse-god'; Taraxippus would be a title of his, not a separate hero.
A fillet is a ribbon or headband, given to victors as a sign of honour.

context_notes.text: Cronos was the father of Jove (the Greek Zeus) and was honoured at Olympia on the hill named for him.
Ilithyia (Eileithyia) was the goddess of childbirth, which fits her joint worship with a child-god.
Elis and Arcadia were neighbouring regions of the Peloponnese and often fought over Olympia and its surroundings.
Ilithyia was the goddess of childbirth; she had a sanctuary at Olympia, and Pausanias is describing monuments in sequence.
The statues paid for by fines were images of Zeus, set up at Olympia from penalties on athletes who cheated.
Cleœtas was an Athenian craftsman; the starting gate he devised was the hippodrome's famous mechanism.
Hercules' campaign against Augeas, king of Elis, is the setting; Cteatus was one of the Molionid twins who fought for Elis.
Orpheus was the legendary musician whose song moved beasts and trees; Amphion's lyre made stones build the walls of Thebes.
The Isthmus is the Isthmus of Corinth, site of the Isthmian Games, where chariot racing also took place.
Nemea in Argolis hosted the Nemean Games, another of the great Greek athletic festivals.

literary_notes.text: The Eleans place a naked infant as their front line, a seemingly absurd defence that proves decisive.
The child's transformation into a dragon shows divine power hidden in apparent weakness; the serpent was a common emblem of protective powers.
Comparing the starting-place to a ship's prow gives the reader a clear picture of its pointed shape, with its "beak" facing the course.
The brief, dramatic sentence shifts from technical description to excitement, as the guide-writer turns attention to the contest itself.
The inscription in Cleœtas's own voice shows his pride in the invention, supporting Pausanias's remark that he plumed himself.
The vivid picture of smashed chariots and injured drivers conveys the real danger and the sense of unexplained dread.
Pausanias reports the Egyptian's account at second hand, keeping a cautious, investigative distance from the claim.
Pausanias reveals his rationalizing, judicious temperament by weighing many stories and choosing the one he finds most plausible.
The statue shows Hippodamia about to crown the man who won her by killing suitors, a quietly ironic ending to the catalogue of deaths.
